analysis.one_liner: Quadruples the excise tax corporations pay when they buy back their own stock.
analysis.headline: Seven Democratic senators proposed quadrupling the 1% tax on corporate stock buybacks and closing an executive-pay offset; the bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since June 2026 with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already imposes a 1% excise tax on corporations that repurchase their own stock, a practice that returns cash to shareholders. This bill would raise that tax to 4% on buybacks after enactment. It would also close an offset: under current law, corporations can reduce the tax by the value of stock they issue to executives, and the bill would end that reduction for highly paid executives and covered employees.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal Treasury and taxpayers generally, because the tax falls on corporations and their largest shareholders rather than on wages or consumer purchases. It also discourages companies from pairing buybacks with large executive stock payouts, since stock issued to executives earning over $1 million would no longer reduce the tax.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the excise tax on corporate stock repurchases from 1% to 4%, applying to buybacks made after the date of enactment.

Ends the current reduction that lets corporations offset the buyback tax by the value of stock issued to covered employees or to anyone paid more than $1 million a year, so buyback-plus-executive-stock strategies no longer shrink the tax.
Sets the new rules to take effect immediately upon enactment, with transition rules for the ongoing tax year, rather than delaying for years.

analysis.who_pays: Large public companies that repurchase stock and their biggest shareholders. Companies could also respond by paying dividends instead of buying back stock, which would shift some of the cost to shareholders, including retirement savers who own stock through pension and 401(k) plans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large public companies and big shareholders

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to all repurchases, and companies can shift from buybacks to dividends or other uses of cash, so part of the burden lands on shareholders generally, including ordinary retirement savers who hold stock through pension funds.
The bill raises revenue but does not dedicate it to any program or worker benefit, so any gain for ordinary people comes only through the general Treasury, not directly.

A higher buyback tax does not guarantee companies will spend the money on wages or investment instead; how firms respond is debated, and some economists argue buybacks can be a legitimate way to return capital when good investment options are limited.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is narrowly aimed at concentrated interests: corporations that repurchase stock and executives paid over $1 million lose a tax break, while no wage earner or consumer pays the tax directly. The main weakness is that the benefit to ordinary people is indirect — general revenue with no dedicated use — and shareholders of all kinds, including retirement savers, could absorb part of the cost if companies shift to dividends.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no further action on it, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the Stock Buyback Accountability Act of 2026 on June 16, 2026, joined by six Democratic colleagues: Wyden, Warren, Reed, Van Hollen, Markey, and Whitehouse.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and the public record shows no markup, hearing, or floor action since.
All seven sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on.
Republicans hold the Senate majority in the 119th Congress, so the Finance Committee is chaired by a Republican who controls whether the bill gets a markup.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that repurchase stock and highly paid executives are better off so far, because the current 1% tax and the executive-stock offset remain unchanged while the bill sits without action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations and highly paid executives

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to quadruple the buyback excise tax and close the executive-stock offset.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; as the senior Democrat on the committee the bill was referred to, his support did not produce a markup.

for.name: Sens. Warren, Reed, Van Hollen, Markey, and Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors the day of introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 16, 2026 and has not scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote since.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; with Republicans holding the Senate majority and chairing the Finance Committee, the bill faces an all-but-one-party path.

analysis.trajectory: With the Senate under Republican control and the Finance Committee chaired by a Republican, a standalone bill with no Republican cosponsors is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote before this Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Its only realistic path would be attachment to a larger tax package, and absent that, it will likely die in committee at the end of the session.
